stories.title_en: A plea not to use uv-build

comments.author: woodruffw
comments.text:
To copy my response on Lobsters:
(I am one of uv’s maintainers.)
The nice thing about Python packaging is that it’s standardized: if uv’s build backend doesn’t fit into the hole you want, then you can use any number of other backends that do an admirable job of conforming to the packaging standards.
With that said, I don’t understand why Gentoo needs to rebuild every single release of uv-build. It doesn’t change as much as uv itself, and it’s intentionally compatible across uv versions. Why not set a policy of only updating once weekly, or even less frequently, with exceptions for important breaking changes or bug fixes?
(For context: the only reason uv-build releases as often as it does is because it’s easier to keep its internals in lockstep with the rest of uv. But you can do a normal version bound in your Python build backend metadata and uv will happily use whatever version of uv-build is already present.)

comments.author: switz
comments.text:
There is so much spam, abuse, and aggressive scraping that I've had to block:
- AWS

- Azure

and a handful of other ASNs on almost all of my properties. It would be one thing if it was simple scraping, but it's often genuine agentic abuse (just spamming for vulnerabilities* or scraping millions of pages with very little valuable or dynamic content). These clouds must get the abuse happening under their own roof under control.
I banned Alibaba's Cloud two years ago and it still hits one of my domains 1 million times per day, despite every route 4xx-ing during that time.
Even Apple has aggressively ramped up its scraping in the past few months, but thankfully they do respect robots.txt.
It's frustrating because some of my real users route through these clouds via their work VPNs. Also, there are a lot of less-than-reputable AI scrapers using global bot-nets via residential IPs to scrape, making it even harder to detect and ban them without affecting real people.
* like leaked .env routes, brute forcing admin panels, and so on

stories.title_en: Hittite royal archive found in Turkey

comments.author: schleck8
comments.text:
The Hittites were one of the largest empires in the ancient world, but up until the last two centuries, the only proper documentation of them was in the Bible, which is why many historians suspected that they were a fictional civilization.
In 1834, French archaelogist Texier found the ruins of their capital Hattusa in modern day Turkey. But he assumed it was Pteria, a city mentioned in ancient Greek documents.
It took another ~ 70 years for German archaelogist Winckler to realize that this was the Hittite capital, based on clay tablets.
